reading_guide.title: Contract audit first
reading_guide.body: The single-current split audit is now the primary HH interpretation surface. Older clean closure, throughput, and aligned-posterior sections should be read as supporting or archival context unless they are revalidated on the same contract.

reading_guide.title: Comparability first
reading_guide.body: Direct clean rows, posterior framework rows, posterior decision rules, hybrid initializers, and active-sequential rows form separate result spaces. Each chart states its own comparison class.

reading_guide.title: Performance versus speedup
reading_guide.body: Performance improvements refer to elapsed time, train time, startup cost, and completed-run throughput. Speedup refers to a ratio against a baseline. The dashboard keeps those quantities separate.

reading_guide.title: Primary versus supporting evidence
reading_guide.body: The Hodgkin-Huxley fixed-task comparison is the empirical center. Benchmark parity, execution studies, and execution-path optimizations support or bound that comparison.

reading_guide.title: Fresh full rerun closure
reading_guide.body: The latest published head completed the full canonical suite from a fresh Falcon clone. That closure matters most for execution, framework, posterior-rule, and surrogate claims, because it turns earlier partial or targeted checks into one end-to-end reproducibility result.

threads.title: Benchmark Parity and Split Integrity
threads.intro: These studies checked whether the inherited FitzHugh-Nagumo baseline remained statistically stable, and whether the archived split behavior remained scientifically interpretable.
threads.how_to_read: Read the metric-delta chart as a bounded difference against the archived benchmark mean, then read the ANOVA chart as a check that node count did not materially change predictive quality.
threads.main_conclusion: The baseline remained statistically close to the archived benchmark, while runtime changed more than predictive quality. The fresh full clean rerun did not change that conclusion, and the split issue still remains an interpretation boundary rather than a moving target.

charts.title: Benchmark deltas against the archived FitzHugh-Nagumo reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate the multi-seed rerun mean was above the archived benchmark value.
notes: The MSE offset is real, but it remains inside the reproduced multi-seed variation envelope.
The R2 shift is very small, which is why the parity conclusion remained positive.

charts.title: Node-count effect test on parity metrics
charts.subtitle: Higher p-values indicate weaker evidence that node count changed model quality.
notes: These p-values support the claim that the benchmark parity result is stable across the tested node counts.
The benchmark study anchors the later systems claims, while remaining supporting evidence rather than a main objective.

threads.title: Execution Configuration and Run Policy
threads.intro: These earlier throughput studies motivated the HH sweep-setting question, but the current HH contract decision is still under audit.
threads.how_to_read: Read these charts as historical support for the execution question, not as a settled answer for the current single-current HH audit surface.
threads.main_conclusion: Earlier throughput packages favored grouped single-node execution, but the dashboard now treats that as supporting context until the single-current split and training audits close.

cards.title: Why this thread moved down
cards.body: The current bundle now foregrounds the split-contract audit. The older throughput packages still matter, because they define plausible candidate sweep settings, but they no longer outrank the contract audit as the main HH interpretation surface.

charts.title: Completed runs per hour, grouped 1-node versus selected 4-node latency path
charts.subtitle: Higher is better. The current Hodgkin-Huxley workload used the right-hand comparison.
notes: On the current Hodgkin-Huxley task, grouped single-node execution improved completed-run throughput by 85.5%.
This chart establishes single-node execution as the broad default, while 4-node latency remains useful for targeted reference runs.

charts.title: Train-time reduction inside the tuned multi-node lane
charts.subtitle: These percentages compare the tuned `R1_accum2_nosync` lane against the earlier node-matched baseline.
notes: These are node-local improvements rather than broad run-policy wins.
This is why performance and speedup should not be conflated in the dashboard text.

charts.title: Final grouped single-node factorization improvement
charts.subtitle: The `factor_s5` path was the last single-node cleanup before the broad default was closed.
notes: This was a small but clean single-node improvement that preserved quality.
Once this path existed, the broad-default case for 4-node execution weakened further.

threads.title: Single-Current Split Contract Audit
threads.intro: These runs compare sequential and random split behavior on the two audited HH current slices while keeping the single-current direct task fixed.
threads.how_to_read: Read the first three charts as the direct HH metric hierarchy that the manuscript now uses, namely paired MAE, mean range-normalized MAE, and empirical marginal Wasserstein. Read the delta chart only as a split-sensitivity summary, not as a family ranking by itself.
threads.main_conclusion: Split choice does not rescue the direct neural row or overturn the classical advantage. The direct DNN row remains stable and much worse than the classical rows on both current slices. Within the classical lane, random forest remains the paired point-accuracy leader, while Extra Trees retains the lower empirical marginal Wasserstein.

cards.title: Current direct audit snapshot
cards.body: At current `0.1`, the direct DNN row stays near MAE `915.4-916.3`, while the classical rows stay near `497-509`. At current `0.3`, the direct DNN row stays near `918.0-920.7`, while the classical rows stay near `492-509`.

cards.title: Direct metric rule
cards.body: The direct HH frontier is no longer read through MAE alone. Paired MAE and mean normalized MAE answer the paired recovery question, while empirical marginal Wasserstein answers whether the predicted population reproduces the held-out parameter marginals in log10 space.

cards.title: Provisional caveat
cards.body: The split audit has completed 27 of 30 rows. The remaining gap is only the last three classical `0.1` random retry rows, so the DNN-versus-classical separation is already stable, but the exact `0.1` classical random means are still slightly provisional.

charts.title: Sequential versus random clean MAE by family and current slice
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. Random bars report the mean across completed random-split rows.
notes: The direct DNN row is nearly unchanged under split choice on both currents.
The classical rows remain much stronger than the direct DNN row under both split policies.

charts.title: Sequential versus random mean normalized MAE by family and current slice
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart asks whether the paired error is large relative to each target's held-out spread.
notes: The normalized view preserves the same separation, which means the direct DNN row is not only worse in absolute units but also worse relative to target scale.
The classical rows stay clustered in the lower normalized-error band on both audited currents.

charts.title: Per-target normalized MAE on the sequential current `0.1` audit slice
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart shows where the direct separation lives inside the target vector.
notes: The classical rows dominate strongly on `hh_param_1`, while the gap narrows but remains across the rest of the target vector.
This is why the manuscript keeps parameter-wise summaries in the direct HH lane.

charts.title: Per-target normalized MAE on the sequential current `0.3` audit slice
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. The per-target pattern remains close to the `0.1` slice.
notes: The direct ranking remains stable target by target on the second audited current slice.
The aggregate direct result is not being driven by one unstable target coordinate.

charts.title: Sequential versus random empirical marginal Wasserstein
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart answers a marginal-fidelity question rather than a paired point-accuracy question.
notes: Extra Trees retains the lower empirical marginal Wasserstein in the classical lane on both currents.
This is why the direct frontier now needs two statements, namely paired point accuracy and marginal fidelity.

charts.title: Random-minus-sequential MAE change
charts.subtitle: Negative values mean the random mean improved over the sequential row.
notes: The direct DNN deltas are effectively zero on both audited currents.
The largest observed split effect is the `+2.20%` MAE penalty for Extra Trees on current `0.3`, which still does not threaten the DNN-versus-classical separation.

threads.title: Posterior-Oriented and Representation Follow-Up
threads.intro: This posterior lane remains descriptive pending re-tabulation on the canonical single-current contract, but the dashboard now reads it through posterior-specific metrics instead of a generic MAE-only summary.
threads.how_to_read: Read the first chart only as point-summary context. Read the later charts as the posterior metric family that the manuscript uses, namely coverage gap, interval width, and truth-centered Wasserstein. These rows are still not the front-door HH claim, because they are not yet regenerated on the current canonical contract.
threads.main_conclusion: Posterior interpretation remains a calibration-and-sharpness tradeoff rather than a single leaderboard. NPSE has the lowest descriptive point-summary MAE in this retained single-current posterior block and the strongest observed coverage, but it pays for that with a much wider `90%` interval, while the other posterior families stay undercovered and only modestly separated on truth-centered Wasserstein.

charts.title: Posterior point-summary MAE by representative family
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart is context only, because it collapses each posterior to one point summary.
notes: NPSE is the strongest descriptive point-summary row by MAE in this retained single-current posterior block.
Point-summary MAE does not establish posterior quality by itself, because it ignores calibration and posterior concentration.

charts.title: Posterior 90% coverage gap by selected rule
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart measures the absolute gap between observed and nominal `90%` coverage.
notes: NPSE has the smallest retained coverage gap in this descriptive block.
The other retained posterior families remain materially undercovered, which is why the manuscript does not treat point-summary MAE as a sufficient posterior metric.

charts.title: Observed posterior coverage by nominal level
charts.subtitle: Higher is not automatically better, because coverage has to be read with interval width, but this chart shows the full multi-level undercoverage pattern.
notes: Rows that approach nominal coverage at `90%` still remain visibly undercovered at the lower nominal levels.
NPSE is strongest on observed coverage, but it achieves that result with a much broader interval.

charts.title: Posterior 90% interval width by selected rule
charts.subtitle: Lower is sharper, but width has to be read together with coverage gap.
notes: NPSE improves the coverage gap only by accepting a much broader posterior interval.
This is the reason the manuscript treats coverage and width as a coupled posterior metric pair.

charts.title: Truth-centered posterior Wasserstein by selected rule
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. Marginal and sliced values answer related but not identical posterior-concentration questions.
notes: The retained single-current posterior families are only modestly separated on truth-centered Wasserstein, which is why the main posterior reading remains a tradeoff rather than a winner-take-all ranking.
The aligned BayesFlow archive remains the cleaner calibration reference, but it belongs to a different, now non-front-door contract.

cards.title: Posterior metric rule
cards.body: This dashboard section now follows the manuscript's posterior metric logic. Point-summary MAE is kept only as context, while coverage gap, interval width, and truth-centered posterior Wasserstein carry the substantive interpretation.

cards.title: Archived aligned BayesFlow context
cards.body: In the archived aligned BayesFlow surface, `bayesflow_meanstd` reaches test MAE `597.7`, coverage gap `0.0198`, interval width `1757.8`, and truth-centered marginal and sliced Wasserstein `0.886` and `0.951`, while `bayesflow_structured` raises MAE to `617.3` but narrows the coverage gap to `0.0107` and lowers empirical marginal Wasserstein to `0.568`. That calibration-sensitive tradeoff still matters interpretively, but it does not define the current admissible HH front door.

cards.title: Aligned archive values
cards.body: The archived aligned reference rows currently retained in the manuscript are `bayesflow_meanstd` test MAE `597.7`, coverage gap `0.0198`, width `1757.8`, and truth-centered marginal and sliced Wasserstein `0.886` and `0.951`. The structured aligned row reaches MAE `617.3`, coverage gap `0.0107`, width `1853.4`, and empirical marginal Wasserstein `0.568`.

threads.title: Shift Robustness and Noise Sensitivity
threads.intro: These studies asked whether the clean winners survived perturbations, and whether shift-specific retraining changed the representative set.
threads.how_to_read: The first chart shows the clean-to-shift-specific posterior interventions. The second chart shows where the robust direct representative gains its practical value.
threads.main_conclusion: Robustness is plural. The fresh clean rerun still says that matched posterior repairs help within their own shift, while the robust direct representative under additive noise is kNN rather than the clean tuned tree.

cards.title: Latest robustness check
cards.body: At additive noise 0.20, `knn_k11` reduced MAE from 916.00 to 510.65 relative to the tuned tree, which is a 44.25% improvement. Inside the posterior family, the drift-specific SNPE retraining row reduced mean-rule MAE from 1135.05 on the clean raw-plus-FFT-plus-summary reference to 1078.92, while the matched mask row reduced it to 1123.65.

charts.title: Shift-specific posterior improvement relative to the clean-trained feature-aware SNPE reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate MAE improvement. The combined-corruption row shows why a single universal corruption-aware model was not promoted.
notes: The positive bars justify shift-specific promoted robustness paths.
The negative combined-corruption bar shows why one pooled robust-SNPE winner would have been misleading.

charts.title: kNN MAE improvement over the tuned tree under additive noise
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate that kNN reduced MAE relative to `extra_trees_500_depth20` at that noise level.
notes: The direct clean winner and the direct robust winner are different, which is why the dashboard keeps them separate at the top.
The improvement stays material even at the heaviest tested additive noise level.

threads.title: Later Executable Extensions
threads.intro: These later executable extensions stay outside the primary direct HH frontier, but the dashboard now reads the active-sequential branch through the same metrics that the manuscript uses.
threads.how_to_read: Read mean absolute log10 error as the primary active-sequential score. Read contraction and ESS together, because sharper concentration without effective posterior support is not a sufficient gain. Read runtime only as operational support.
threads.main_conclusion: Inside the active-sequential branch, disagreement remains the primary error row and also has the strongest posterior contraction, while ESS stays nearly unchanged across the three policies. Wasserstein remains effectively tied on the primary error metric and retains the clearest distribution-aware acquisition interpretation.

charts.title: Active-sequential error metric by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This remains the primary active-sequential score.
notes: Disagreement is the best active-sequential row on the primary error metric.
Wasserstein is only marginally worse on error, which is why the branch remains an interpretive rather than a decisive operational split.

charts.title: Active-sequential posterior contraction
charts.subtitle: Higher indicates tighter concentration under the sequential posterior summary used in this branch.
notes: Disagreement has the strongest contraction in the current active-sequential suite.
The Wasserstein and uncertainty rows remain close to each other on this concentration measure.

charts.title: Active-sequential effective sample size
charts.subtitle: Higher indicates slightly better retained posterior support, but the three policies are nearly tied here.
notes: ESS is nearly unchanged across the three active-sequential policies.
This is why the active-sequential interpretation does not reduce to an ESS-driven distinction.

charts.title: Active-sequential mean relative error
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart is secondary to the log10 error row, but it confirms that the policies remain tightly clustered on a scale-free error view.
notes: Relative error is almost tied across the three active-sequential policies, which is why it remains secondary to the main log10 error metric.
The stronger separation in this branch comes from contraction and interpretive stance rather than from scale-free relative-error magnitude.

charts.title: Active-sequential runtime by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. Runtime remains secondary to the active-sequential metric logic.
notes: The three active-sequential policies stay in the same runtime band.
ASNPE is no longer a runtime outlier, but it remains materially weaker on the primary active-sequential error metric.

cards.title: Metric hierarchy inside the active-sequential branch
cards.body: The manuscript treats this branch as a separate inferential object. Mean absolute log10 parameter error remains the primary score, while contraction and ESS clarify whether similar error levels conceal different posterior concentration behavior.

cards.title: Wasserstein versus disagreement
cards.body: The Wasserstein policy remains within `0.31%` of disagreement on the primary error metric, while ESS stays essentially unchanged and disagreement retains the stronger contraction. The practical choice is therefore mostly interpretive, because Wasserstein keeps the clearest distance-aware acquisition meaning.

threads.title: Execution-Path Optimizations
threads.intro: These studies optimized startup behavior inside the extracted-data Hodgkin-Huxley execution path. They mattered operationally, while the scientific frontier remained unchanged.
threads.how_to_read: The cache charts measure startup reduction inside the execution path. The explanation cards clarify why the branch stayed secondary, even though the later mmap-backed canaries were strong.
threads.main_conclusion: Feature-scale caching reduced preprocessing materially, the mmap-backed split-array cache removed almost all startup overhead in the successful canaries, and the final fresh clean run also confirmed that cache locking and step-local cache isolation are sufficient for concurrent cohorts. The branch is therefore no longer only a canary proof, because it now supports the published concurrent full runner directly.

charts.title: Feature-scale cache preprocessing reduction
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate preprocessing time reduction relative to the eager path.
notes: This optimization attacked a measured startup bottleneck while preserving the eager hot loop.
That is why feature-scale cache became the extracted-data default before split-array caching did.

charts.title: Split-array mmap startup reduction after the proof chain
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate data-load reduction against the completed R4 medians for the same families.
notes: The first split-array canary failed badly, which is why the branch was initially kept experimental.
After the mmap-backed reload fix, the branch cleared both the dedicated launcher proof and a broader ordinary-launcher proof, so the remaining question became marginal value rather than correctness.

cards.title: Why it was not tested as a full campaign
cards.body: The branch ultimately addressed startup overhead inside one extracted-data execution path. By the time the later proofs succeeded, the main systems question had already been answered by the throughput-first single-node policy, and the model-frontier question had already moved into family comparison, representation, and robustness work. The split-array branch was therefore tested enough to establish viability, while a full factorial expansion would have consumed effort without changing the main scientific claims.

cards.title: What was actually proved
cards.body: The later proof chain established that the split-array cache could be prewarmed, launched through its ordinary canary package, exercised through an older ordinary HH launcher, protected by explicit cache-file locking, and isolated per parallel cohort when contention risk existed. That is the execution-path contract which survived the final fresh full clean rerun.
